theme: Coaching as the Core Manager Behavior
title: The Coaching Moment
tagline: Spotting the coaching moment hiding inside the status conversation.
description: A 45-minute virtual session for Vanderbilt managers: learn to catch the coaching moment inside an ordinary status conversation, trade instructions for one good question, and give the talk a simple four-beat shape.
heroLead: Coaching moments arrive mid-1:1, as an aside about the person inside a task update. This session teaches you to catch that aside and coach it instead of solving it.
objectives: Recognize a coaching moment inside an ordinary status conversation
Trade instructions for one good question that puts the thinking in their head
Run a ten-minute coaching talk with a simple four-beat shape
missionTie: Managers who coach grow the people a century-defining university runs on, which makes every coached 1:1 a small act of Exceptional Core Operations.

agenda.d: What a coaching moment sounds like inside a routine status conversation.
Why one good question beats three instructions, and how to find it.
Goal, reality, options, will: four beats that keep a coaching talk moving.

manifesto: When the aside is about the person, ask one open question before you offer anything.

sections.headline: Status updates hide coaching moments.
sections.lead: A coaching moment is the point where the subject stops being the task and becomes the person. It usually arrives mid-update as a small aside, and if you keep driving the task it is gone in ten seconds.
sections.group: In pairs, 90 seconds each: recall an aside from a recent 1:1 you drove past. What was the person really telling you?
sections.solo: Recall an aside from a recent 1:1 you drove past. What was the person really telling you?

deeper.title: Steam or door: telling asides apart
deeper.body: Asides are trial balloons. Saying 'I second-guess every call' straight out feels risky, so people float it sideways and watch what you do with it. Drive past and the test quietly fails; the asides stop coming. One distinction sharpens your ear: steam repeats a complaint about circumstances, a door says something about the person. Steam wants a nod. A door wants one question, and one is usually all you get.
steps: List your 1:1s from the past two weeks and write down every aside about the person you can remember. Roles, never names.
Mark each one steam or door: circumstances, or something about them? Steam gets a nod; a door gets a question.
Pick one door and write the exact sentence you will use to reopen it at your next 1:1.

interaction.context: Picture this morning's 1:1s across Vanderbilt. A coordinator finishes an update, then adds: 'Honestly, I second-guess every one of these decisions.' In most rooms that aside gets quick reassurance or a fix, and the door closes politely before anyone notices it was open.
interaction.discuss: Think of the last aside you drove past in a 1:1. What made it easy to miss, and what was the person really telling you?

card.text: Listen for the sentence about themselves inside the sentences about the task: 'I never know when to escalate.' 'I hate presenting these.' The update carries the work; the aside carries the person. The aside is the door.

interaction.q: A coordinator finishes an update, then adds: 'Honestly, I second-guess every one of these decisions.' What just happened?

opts.t: A confidence wobble you should reassure away
opts.why: Reassurance closes the door politely. 'You're doing fine' ends the conversation the aside was trying to start.

opts.t: A coaching moment: the subject just became their judgment
opts.why: Right. The update was about the task; the aside is about them. That is the door, and it stays open for about one question.

opts.t: A request for you to review their decisions from now on
opts.why: Taking the decisions back solves this week and shrinks the person. They pointed at growth and heard you offer supervision.

sections.headline: One question beats three instructions.
sections.lead: Telling is fast and works once. A question works from then on, because the thinking happens in their head. Ibarra and Scoular call this the heart of coaching: drawing insight out instead of handing answers down.
sections.group: In pairs: take an instruction you gave this week and rewrite it together as one open question. Trade and improve.
sections.solo: Take an instruction you gave this week and rewrite it as one open question.

source.label: The Leader as Coach, Herminia Ibarra and Anne Scoular (Harvard Business Review, 2019)

deeper.title: The second question
deeper.body: The first question opens the thinking; the second decides who keeps it. Whatever they answer, go one layer down before you evaluate anything: 'what makes that the hard part?' or 'what happened when you tried it?' First answers are usually the safe ones; the real material sits underneath. And when their plan is worse than yours, name the gap you see and ask what they would do about it. Graded answers dry up fast.
steps: Put three stems where you run 1:1s: 'What have you tried?' 'What is the hard part?' 'What would you do if I were out this week?'
In your next stuck conversation, ask one stem, then follow the answer one layer down before you offer anything of your own.

interaction.intro: A team member brings you a stuck. Read what the manager says back and call it.
labels: Telling: the manager keeps the thinking
Asking: the thinking goes to them
Fake question: an instruction in disguise
interaction.passMsg: You can hear the difference. Real questions hand the thinking over; disguised instructions just soften the telling.
interaction.failMsg: Close. The tell: if you already know the answer you want, it is telling, whatever the punctuation says.

items.q: 'This vendor keeps missing deadlines.' Manager: 'Call them today and copy procurement.'
items.why: Clear, fast, and the manager keeps the thinking. Fine for a fire; done every time, it trains the team to bring problems raw.

items.q: 'I can't get the two directors to agree.' Manager: 'What have you already tried, and what happened?'
items.why: Genuinely open. The manager does not know the answer yet, and the question makes the person walk their own reality before anyone offers options.

items.q: 'I'm behind on the report.' Manager: 'Don't you think you should have started earlier?'
items.why: The question mark is decoration. There is one acceptable answer, so it lands as a scolding. If you know the answer you want, say it plainly or ask something real.

sections.headline: Four beats keep the talk moving.
sections.lead: A coaching talk without a shape wanders. Sir John Whitmore's GROW model gives it one: where are they trying to get (goal), what is happening (reality), what could they try (options), what will they do (will). Plain words, their answers, ten minutes.

source.label: The GROW model, Sir John Whitmore (Performance Consultants)

deeper.title: Where the four beats stall
deeper.body: Each beat has a classic stall. Goal: taking the first answer at face value; ask what reaching it would actually get them. Reality: rushing it, which is where most bad options are born. Options: stopping at one; push for three before choosing, since even a weak third loosens the thinking. Will: a commitment without a date, which is a wish. The Canaday course and the GROW practicum are live reps for whichever beat stalls on you.
steps: Pick a real stuck on your team and write one question per beat before the next 1:1. Four lines, plain words.
Run the talk, then note which beat stalled. That beat is your rep to practice next time.
Start the Canaday course on LinkedIn Learning or book a navigator-led GROW practicum slot this week.

interaction.intro: An advisor on your team says: 'I want the senior cases, and I keep getting passed over.' Coach it in two moves.

opts.t: Explain how case assignments actually get decided.
opts.coach: Information is telling in its Sunday clothes. They leave knowing the process and still holding the want with nowhere to put it.

opts.t: Ask: 'Have you told the assignments lead you want them?'
opts.coach: A real question that jumps straight to one option. You picked the route before you knew where they are trying to go.

opts.t: Ask: 'What would the senior cases mean for where you're headed?'
opts.coach: Goal first. Before options make sense, both of you need to hear what they are actually reaching for; sometimes the cases are a proxy for something else.

opts.t: Offer to raise it with the assignments lead yourself.
opts.coach: Rescue feels generous and takes the ball away. Next time they are passed over, the skill still lives with you.

opts.t: Ask what is in the way, then hand them your best fix.
opts.coach: Reality, then a telling. Better; still, the options were yours. Ask for theirs first and add yours only if the well runs dry.

opts.t: Ask what they could try, then which one they will do by Friday.
opts.coach: Options, then will, in their words. The commitment they name aloud, with a date, is the part of coaching that survives the meeting.

heads.strong: A ten-minute talk that grew someone. They left with their own plan and a date, and you left knowing what they actually want.
heads.mid: Helpful, and mostly yours. The person got movement this week and no more ownership than they walked in with.
heads.weak: The task got handled; the person got skipped. They will bring you the same stuck again, because the thinking stayed with you.

reactions.strong: Friday comes and they did the thing they named, because they named it. A month later they are handling assignment conversations without you, and the want you surfaced is shaping their next role.
reactions.mid: Your fix worked, which is the problem: they learned that stuck things go to you. The next want arrives the same way, still raw, still yours to solve.
reactions.weak: The assignments lead never hears from them. The want goes quiet, and quiet wants are how next quarter's flight risks get made.

recap.q: Mid-update, a team member adds: 'I always freeze when leadership pushes back.' That is...
opts: A coaching moment: the subject just became them
A performance issue for the annual review
A cue to reassure and move on
recap.why: The sentence about the person inside the sentences about the task is what a coaching moment sounds like, and it rarely comes twice.

recap.q: Why does one good question beat three instructions?
opts: Questions take less time to give
The thinking happens in their head and stays there
recap.why: Telling works once. A real question builds the judgment they will use when you are nowhere near the problem.

recap.q: The four beats of a simple coaching talk, in order...
recap.why: Where they are headed, what is true now, what they could try, what they will do. Their words at every beat, and the will beat gets a date.

recapMsgs.high: The ear is tuned. Now aim it at one real aside from your own team.
recapMsgs.mid: Solid. Revisit the section you missed, then build your card.
recapMsgs.low: Worth a second pass through the three sections before you commit.

capstone.headline: One aside. One question. This week.
capstone.lead: Pick the person whose aside you have been driving past. Role only, never a name; nothing you type is saved or sent.
capstone.whoLabel: Whose coaching moment do you owe? Role and the aside you remember.
capstone.whoPlaceholder: e.g. research coordinator; 'I never know when to escalate'

practices.name: Reopen the door
practices.move: Bring the aside back: 'Last week you mentioned second-guessing those calls. Say more?' Then stay quiet.

practices.name: The one question
practices.move: At the next stuck, trade your instruction for one open question you do not know the answer to.

practices.name: The ten-minute talk
practices.move: Run the four beats end to end: goal, reality, options, will, and let them name the date.

whens.out: The moment gets coached this week, in whichever conversation hands it to you first.
Your next 1:1 opens with the aside, first item, before any status updates.
The coaching talk happens within two weeks, with the 1:1 extended ten minutes so it fits.

capstone.evidenceRow: Afterward, one line: what did they figure out that you did not have to tell them?

closing.headline: Coach one aside this week.
closing.lead: This week, bring back the aside on your card and ask one open question. The rest of the week gives everyone, managers included, the record in Oracle and the listening underneath coaching.
closing.nextTag: Your one next step · This week
closing.nextTitle: Coach the moment on your card
closing.nextBody: Run it exactly as built: bring back the aside, ask the question, let them name the will. Bring one line about what they figured out to next Monday.
closing.brandline: Trade one instruction for one question.

facilitator.audience: Vanderbilt people managers and team leads in the Anchor's Edge weekly rhythm. Works for 6 to 40 on a call; breakouts run in pairs. No prerequisites; March is the Coaching as the Core Manager Behavior month, putting December's manager standard into daily practice, and this session opens the week.
facilitator.pulse: Seven days out, send the pulse: 'Did you catch the moment on your card? What did the person figure out without being told? What aside are you listening for next?' Count of coached moments feeds the manager-standard behavior metric for the month.

s1.title: The moment in the middle
s1.purpose: Teach managers to hear the coaching moment: the aside about the person inside the talk about the task.
s1.say: Most 1:1s run as status meetings, and most of the time that is right; the task deserves managing. But somewhere in the middle of the updates, people hand you a sentence about themselves, an aside like 'I second-guess every one of these calls.' Most of us drive right past it because the task is louder. This section trains your ear to stop for it.
facilitate: Read the concept card aloud once; the two aside examples do the teaching.
Share the In the room card and let the coordinator's aside land; ask what usually happens next in real rooms.
Run the discussion prompt, then the breakout on the aside they drove past, 90 seconds each way.

ask.q: What did the last aside you drove past sound like?
expect: Quotes like 'I always mess this up' or 'I hate this part'
Some managers cannot remember one, which is itself the point
ask.respond: Both answers teach. If asides come easily, the ear exists and needs aiming. If none surface, the task has been drowning out the person, and this week is for listening differently.

s1.debrief: Coaching moments are handed to you mid-task, as an aside about the person, and you usually get one question in before the door swings shut.
s1.watchFor: Managers who hear 'coach everything.' Be plain: most of the 1:1 stays task, and that is right. The skill is catching the one moment that is about the person.
s1.transition: You caught the moment. What you say next decides who does the thinking.
s1.coreNote: Core: skip the breakout; ask for one remembered aside in chat instead.

s2.title: Ask before you tell
s2.purpose: Replace the instruction reflex with one genuinely open question that transfers the thinking.
s2.say: So the door is open, and the reflex now is to be useful: three instructions, problem handled, next agenda item. Herminia Ibarra and Anne Scoular wrote about this shift in HBR as The Leader as Coach. Their argument is that no manager has all the answers anymore, so the job becomes asking questions that draw insight out of the person in front of you. What a good question starts in someone's head stays theirs afterward. That is worth more than your three instructions.
facilitate: Run Tell or ask? live; everyone plays on their own screen.
After round three, pause on the fake question; ask the room where they have heard one this month.
Run the breakout: rewrite one real instruction as one open question.

ask.q: What makes the fake question in round three worse than plain telling?
expect: It pretends to hand over the thinking while keeping it
It adds judgment on top of the instruction
People learn to hear every question as a trap
ask.respond: All three. Plain telling is at least honest about what it is. A fake question spends trust, and trust is what your real questions will need.

s2.debrief: If you already know the answer you want, it is telling. Say it honestly, or ask something you genuinely cannot answer for them.
s2.watchFor: Managers hunting for the perfect question. Lower the bar: 'what have you tried?' and 'what would you do if I were out this week?' cover most moments.
s2.transition: One question opens the thinking. A light shape keeps it moving.
s2.coreNote: Core: run the trainer, skip the breakout, take one rewrite aloud.

s3.title: A shape for the talk
s3.purpose: Give the coaching talk a four-beat shape in plain words: goal, reality, options, will.
s3.say: A coaching talk needs a shape or it wanders. Here is one in plain words: where are they trying to get, what is actually going on, what could they try, what will they do. Sir John Whitmore named it GROW decades ago and serious coaching still runs on it; you need the order, and the last beat needs a date. If you want deeper reps, this month's LinkedIn Learning pick is Sara Canaday's Coaching Skills for Leaders and Managers, and the navigator-led GROW practicum runs alongside it. Optional, and worth it.
facilitate: Run Coach the moment; two minutes for both choices, then run it.
Ask one volunteer to read their outcome aloud, weak or strong.
Point at the pattern: goal before options, their options before yours, a will with a date.

ask.q: Why does the rescue move in slot two feel so right and work so badly?
expect: It is fast and feels generous
It takes the ball, so the skill never transfers
ask.respond: Exactly. Rescue solves this week and buys next month's version of the same stuck. Coaching is slower once so it can be faster forever.

s3.debrief: Goal, reality, options, will. Their words at every beat, and the will beat leaves with a date attached.
s3.watchFor: Managers running the four beats as an interrogation checklist. It is a shape for listening; two beats done well beat four beats done fast.
s3.transition: Quick recap, then you pick your moment and build the card.
s3.coreNote: Core: everyone runs the builder solo; skip the read-aloud.

facilitator.capstoneSay: Now make it real. One person whose aside you have been driving past, role only. Pick how you will coach it, pick the window, build the card, and copy it somewhere you will see it before your next 1:1. Two minutes, quiet, go.
facilitator.closeSay: You leave with an ear for the aside, one real question, and a four-beat shape. Coach the moment on your card this week. Tomorrow's Take-Off Tuesday is for everyone, you included: capturing development goals and coaching notes in Oracle, so the growth you coach goes on the record. Thursday's Thrive Thursday builds the empathy underneath all of it, hearing what isn't said. And if you want more reps, Sara Canaday's Coaching Skills for Leaders and Managers is this month's LinkedIn Learning pick, with the navigator-led GROW practicum alongside it.

contingencies.if: Screen share or the site fails mid-session
contingencies.then: Paste the learner link in chat and narrate from your own browser; every interaction runs on learner devices without the share.
Run the breakout prompts as 60-second chat storms: everyone types their answer at once, you read the best three aloud.

contingencies.if: A manager names a real team member while sharing an aside
contingencies.then: Protect them warmly and immediately: 'Hold that. Roles, never names.' Coaching moments belong to the person; a group call is never the place to spend one.

contingencies.if: A manager insists telling is faster and coaching is a luxury
contingencies.then: Agree, once. Telling wins the moment; coaching wins the quarter. Do the math aloud: ten minutes of coaching against the tenth repeat of the same stuck.

toughQuestions.q: What if I ask a good question and get silence?
toughQuestions.a: Let it sit for five full seconds; silence usually means thinking, and filling it takes the thinking back. If it truly stalls, shrink the question: 'what is one thing you have tried?' A smaller true answer beats a bigger rescued one.

toughQuestions.q: Isn't GROW just another corporate acronym?
toughQuestions.a: It has better roots than most: Sir John Whitmore built it in the 1980s and it remains the backbone of professional coaching. Treat it as an order, never a script: what they want, what is true, what they could try, what they will do. You can run all four beats without ever saying the word GROW.

toughQuestions.q: What if the aside is really a performance problem?
toughQuestions.a: Coaching and performance management are different conversations, and both are yours. If the gap is willingness or repeated missed standards, name it directly through the performance process. Coach the growth asides; never use coaching questions to hint at a problem you owe them plainly.

templates.title: Pre-work invite (paste into the calendar invite)
templates.body: Subject: Monday, 45 minutes on catching coaching moments. Bring the memory of one recent 1:1 that stayed on status the whole way through. You will never be asked to name anyone. Live and interactive; have the session link open on your own screen.

templates.title: 7-day pulse (send one week after)
templates.body: Subject: Did you catch the moment? Three lines, reply whenever: 1) Did the coaching moment on your card happen? 2) What did the person figure out without being told? 3) What aside are you listening for next?
